entries.title: Democrats Want a DCCC Reset After Three High-Profile Losses
entries.summary: House Democrats say the stinging losses could threaten everything from the DCCC’s ability to win in general elections to its ability to collect member dues.
entries.content:
Some House Democrats want the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee to rethink its primary strategy after its third high-profile loss this season.

The 2026 election is far from over, but Democrats are already making specific demands for the DCCC to consider in future cycles: The committee needs to improve how it communicates with members, find ways to take more feedback and stop interfering in Democratic primaries.

House Democrats have heavily criticized their campaign arm over its involvement in primaries during an election cycle that has been defined by anti-establishment sentiment. This week, DCCC-backed Marlene Galán-Woods lost the primary in Arizona’s 1st Congressional District to Amish Shah, the latest in a stinging set of losses for the group.

“I think that it should certainly result in a pretty significant reevaluation of the strategy, the decision-making and the approach around primary endorsements and support,” one House Democrat, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly, told NOTUS. “The leadership of DCCC has a fiduciary responsibility to reevaluate things, given the several notable examples of non-DCCC-supported candidates winning.”

The lawmaker added that members who pay dues to the DCCC “would have much greater confidence if we feel like there's a genuine reevaluation of this approach.”

Other House Democrats echoed the sentiment.

“There's no reason for us to put our thumb on the scale when you have a healthy field of many viable candidates,” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) told NOTUS.

Ocasio-Cortez said the DCCC believes that “one type of candidate, or one type of approach, or one type of ideology is what will win in every swing seat in America.” Instead, she said, what the committee needs “to be doing is have an approach that is more tailored and is listening to every community.”

Before Galán-Woods lost her race, Maine state Sen. Joe Baldacci lost to progressive Matt Dunlap in that state’s 2nd Congressional District, and California Assembly member Jasmeet Bains lost to another progressive, Randy Villegas, in the 22nd Congressional District.

To some Democrats, these races illustrate breakdowns in the way the DCCC communicates with its members and allies.

For example, the DCCC failed to inform the Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC that it was adding Bains to its “Red to Blue” flagship candidate program before she won her primary, even though the committee had agreed to keep the CPC PAC informed about its decisions, according to multiple sources.

The CPC PAC only found out about the DCCC’s move the day before it was announced — and only because Villegas heard about it in California and then called the progressive group, which was backing him.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), a CPC PAC co-chair, told NOTUS that the progressive group “immediately set up a call” with DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries after learning about their involvement.

They “apologized profusely,” Jayapal said, and “said it never should have happened that way, it was an oversight.”

“I think it begs the question of engaging in any Democratic primary,” Jayapal added. “At a minimum, if they’re going to engage, we need to know if we have a candidate in that race, and we need to have a really thoughtful discussion about it.”

The DCCC did add Villegas to its “Red to Blue” program after he defeated Bains in June, and a spokesperson for his campaign told NOTUS in a statement that since the primary, “DCCC has been extremely helpful in our shared goal of defeating David [Valadao].”

But the miscommunication around the DCCC’s primary involvement came at a time when the CPC PAC “is mobilizing our members to give the most amount of DCCC dues we’ve ever given,” said Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Florida), another CPC PAC co-chair.

If the DCCC doesn’t change its election strategy, it runs the risk of members not paying their dues to the committee. Dues are already being affected by redistricting, which has cut the number of members who pay the party’s campaign arm, as NOTUS first reported.

“It makes you think, ‘I’m giving my dues to win in November, not for primaries,’ and so you’d think it could discourage members from giving dues,” Frost said.

In a statement to NOTUS, DCCC communications director Courtney Rice defended the group’s involvement in the primaries.

“When the DCCC decides to put a candidate in a competitive primary on Red to Blue, it is done after polling and research into different general election match-ups and discussions with Caucus members, local leaders, labor, and other stakeholders,” Rice said. “Given Democrats’ big tent, there is not always consensus, but the decisions are never made in a vacuum.”

Under the leadership of DelBene, the DCCC has been involved in 10 contested primaries in 2026 and won seven. But the three losses have been high profile enough to take up much of the oxygen, and opened the group to attacks. Republicans' campaign arm put out a press release Wednesday calling DCCC’s most recent primary loss a “humiliation.”

“I have complete and total confidence in Suzan DelBene, her leadership of the DCCC, and as a result of that leadership, I’m confident we’re going to take back control of the House of Representatives in November,” Jeffries said at a press conference Thursday when asked about DCCC’s involvement in primaries.

Some members said there’s a desire in the caucus for the DCCC to create more avenues for members to provide feedback to the committee.

Rep. Sydney Kamlager-Dove (D-California) told NOTUS the DCCC needs to “listen to members from the states where candidates are running to really understand what's happening on the ground, to understand the local dynamics, and to either support the candidates that are best connected to the community, or to let the dynamics play out in the primary.”

The DCCC, Kamlager-Dove said, holds regular “listening sessions” where members can keep the committee informed about “what they’re seeing, what’s happening” in their states.

However, attendance does not appear to be mandatory; when asked if the DCCC seemed receptive to the feedback from those meetings, the lawmaker said, “I couldn't say because honestly, I don't join many of them. I stay focused on my own state and how I can be helpful to the ‘Red to Blue’ candidates that are running.”

Some House Democrats are floating the idea of creating a committee that gives members more say over the DCCC’s decisions. Axios first reported lawmakers’ interest in a formal body to give that feedback.

“It would not be a bad idea for us to really consider what leadership will look like that's beyond one person,” Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Illinois), an outspoken critic of the DCCC’s involvement in primaries, told NOTUS. “A coordinated approach, a table convening of six or seven members of Congress, that represent different parts of this big tent that can help provide adequate, intentional perspectives as they're making their decision.”

“One person can’t possibly have the breadth of understanding and the dynamics of what’s happening on the ground,” Ramirez added. “I certainly want to talk about that as we're thinking about how we move next year.”

The DCCC’s primary election strategy has also been criticized by Democratic candidates.

Joe Caiazzo, a consultant for Dunlap’s campaign in Maine, told NOTUS that the DCCC “has made some decisions this cycle that have been far from ideal.”

But, he added, “as we march towards November, we all need to unify in an effort to win back the House, and I think that there are many competitive races around the country that the DCCC could absolutely come to the table and support to ensure that we are broadening the map.”

While Dunlap painted himself as an anti-establishment candidate during his primary, Caiazzo said Dunlap is still interested in getting the DCCC’s backing — highlighting how the party’s support remains valuable for the general election.

“We’re talking to the DCCC, we have a good relationship, and I expect that they will eventually move him to ‘Red to Blue,’” Caiazzo said.

In a statement released after the Arizona race was called Wednesday, Shah similarly touted his win as a “grassroots victory where Arizona voters made their voices heard,” adding that the “status quo in Washington, D.C., is not working for Arizonans.”

The day before, he’d told reporters that if he won the race, “I’m sure we’ll have a phone call, and I will speak to the DCCC and I hope that I can get their endorsement.”

“Any Democratic candidate would want to be on the ‘Red to Blue’ list,” a source close to Shah’s campaign told NOTUS.

It is unlikely that the DCCC will stop becoming involved in Democratic primaries.

Dan Sena, the DCCC’s executive director in the 2018 cycle, pointed to the Maine Senate race, where Graham Platner stepped down as the Democratic nominee after being accused of sexual assault — which he denies — as an example of what happens when “you allow things to just happen without heavy input.”

“You either get involved in the primaries and you win seven out of 10, or you don't get involved and you come up shy in the majority,” Sena said. “Either way, the Democrats have to ask themselves, wouldn't you rather have the gavels in your hand?"

entries.title: Democrats Lock Back In on Maine
entries.summary: Whether they can win is an open question.
entries.content:
Maine Democrats are on track to select a new Senate candidate later this week. Their likely pick? A former state lawmaker who lost the party’s recent gubernatorial primary, has no federal political experience and has only three months to assemble a campaign against a 30-year Republican incumbent.

Most party leaders — including Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, who said she’s “very optimistic that we will win Maine” — say they haven’t felt this good about the race in months.

“I think it's going to be hotly contested, but I think it's very much back in play,” said Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico.

On Saturday, Democrats in Maine are expected to pick Troy Jackson as their Senate nominee against Republican incumbent Susan Collins, less than a month after the party’s former nominee, Graham Platner, was accused of sexual assault, the latest in a string of controversies he faced throughout his campaign.

Jackson’s nomination would cap what has been one of the party’s most tumultuous primary processes in recent memory, a series of mishaps that could — and is widely expected to — jeopardize the Democrats’ ability to defeat Collins.

That’s especially the case with a candidate like Jackson, who even allies acknowledge is an underwhelming orator with little time to build out a campaign infrastructure.

But Democrats in Washington and Maine insist they think he’s still in a better position than Platner, who, despite denying the allegations, carried baggage into the race that party strategists feared would undermine his electability.

“Turbulence is never the friend of politics, but I think there’s plenty of time,” Sen. John Hickenlooper of Colorado told NOTUS. “There's some history, and people have done attack ads, and you know, have in some way vetted him a little more thoroughly than some candidates get.”

The sentiment reflects just how anxious many Democrats — especially moderates — had become about Platner’s chances against Collins, so much so that they are relieved to throw in with a candidate few national Democrats know well.

More importantly, it indicates that Democrats remain committed to trying to win the Senate race despite everything that has happened there. Democrats likely need to win the race in Maine — the only Senate seat held by a Republican in a state won by Kamala Harris in 2024 that is up for grabs this year — to have a chance at flipping majority control of the Senate.

Platner’s baggage had made his path to victory “very likely insurmountable,” said Lauren French, spokesperson for Senate Majority PAC, a super PAC aligned with Senate Democrats.

“Now we have the opportunity to refocus this conversation where it should be, which is Susan Collins,” she said.

National Democrats have pointedly stayed out of the race to replace Platner. Asked if he would support Jackson, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer expressed confidence in defeating Collins, a formidable and well-funded incumbent who is seeking her sixth term in Washington.

“We're going to win Maine. Susan Collins is going to lose, and we are going to take back the Senate,” Schumer told NOTUS. “People in Maine don't like Donald Trump, and they don't like that Susan Collins always votes with him.”

Jackson told The New York Times this week that he would not support Schumer being the party’s leader in the Senate. He was also wary of receiving support from the minority leader.

“I’d have to find out what that entailed,” Jackson told the New York Times. “I mean, if his help comes, absolutely no strings, I would say, you know, possibly. There’d have to be no strings.”

Jackson’s team did not comment for this article.

Among voters, Jackson, a fifth-generation logger and former state Senate president, appears to start the race in a competitive position. He edged out Collins by 3 percentage points in a recent poll from the University of New Hampshire, and, unlike Collins, he is viewed quite favorably by Maine voters. The poll’s margin of error is 2.8 percentage points.

But that could change with the onslaught of Republican attacks waiting for him in the general election.

Republicans have already begun drawing parallels between Platner and Jackson. They’ve pointed to Jackson’s reported history of growing angry in meetings, and attacked him for views Republicans have cast as extreme, like support for a single-payer health care system.

“He's had quite a transformation over the years in his political views, but now seems to be firmly aligned with the democratic socialists,” Collins told NBC News, referring to Jackson’s conservative positions on social issues, like abortion, more than a decade ago.

Democrats acknowledge that Maine will still be a difficult place for Democrats to win, but President Donald Trump’s unpopularity and rising costs give the party a chance to make a compelling case.

“While the Democrats will have a new candidate by the end of this weekend, the fundamental motivation around winning the Senate race hasn't changed at all,” said Emily Cain, a Democratic strategist in Maine.

Platner’s departure is a second chance at the seat without the distraction of controversy, some Democrats argue.

An open question is whether Jackson can raise the money needed to beat Collins, who had nearly $11 million in the bank at the end of June. He’s raised $1 million in the less than two weeks since he entered the race, Politico reported.

“All 49 states of Democratic Party activists and donors — small donors and large donors — are now all eyes on Maine,” said Democratic strategist Mike Trujillo.

One Democratic donor who gave the largest contribution they could to Graham Platner told NOTUS they plan to give the maximum donation to the new candidate as well.

“Maine is Maine,” the donor said. “My priority is winning in the general in every state where we're competitive, and that definitely includes Maine. No matter who's running, I'm sold.”

Still, other Democrats are less than certain about their chances of flipping Maine’s Senate seat after Platner’s collapse and the rushed process for selecting his replacement.

“They had to come up with somebody, and they did,” Hawaii Sen. Mazie Hirono said of Maine Democrats’ likely nomination of Jackson.

Asked if he had a better shot than Platner, Hirono burst into laughter.

“Let's just say that we have a candidate,” she said.

entries.title: The Mystics Are Officially a Problem for the Rest of the WNBA
entries.summary: Washington closed the first half of its season with a win over the powerhouse Aces, further proving it is a legitimate contender.
entries.content:
The transcontinental stretch of games that closed out the first half of the Washington Mystics’ 2026 season could best be described as Odyssean: six contests across 11 days, half of them against the top tier of WNBA opponents, and requiring four flights and nearly 6,500 air miles to navigate before they finally reached home. Along the way, the league’s youngest team faced nearly everything short of cyclopses, cannibals and sirens.

What to make, then, of head coach Sydney Johnson revealing late Wednesday that the top item on his All-Star break bucket list — apart from family time, a little film work and some couch-side viewing of Saturday night’s WNBA All-Star Game — is to take in the new epic remake of “The Odyssey” with his wife?

“I just really want to see that movie,” Johnson shrugged, with something short of Homeric grandeur.

Truth is, he doesn’t need to see it. He just lived it.

By the time the Mystics had slain the last beast on their own odyssey — taking down the defending champion Las Vegas Aces, 100-99, at home Wednesday night to complete that grueling, six-game stretch with a 4-2 record — it was the rest of the WNBA that was collectively waking up to a realization:

The Mystics are officially a problem.

Despite having the second-youngest roster in league history, they arrive at the All-Star break, and on the cusp of the Aug. 2 trade deadline, with a 14-12 record, far above most preseason predictions and good for the eighth and final playoff spot if the season ended today. Even more impressive is the way they closed out the first half: with back-to-back wins at Golden State and at home against Las Vegas — the No. 2 and No. 3 teams in the W, respectively — in a 72-hour stretch, with a cross-country flight in between.

“They’re very long. They're athletic. They're well-coached. I’m not surprised they're sitting where they're sitting,” Aces coach Becky Hammon said of the Mystics. “They don't go away. They hang around in games, which always gives you a chance to win. There is a skillset in winning together, and even though this team is young they're proving that they're developing [the ability] to win tough games down the stretch.

“Their length and their physicality and athleticism are [elite]. I don't think too many teams in this league can deal with that.”

On Wednesday night, the Mystics pummeled Hammon’s Aces inside and out. Washington’s three bigs — 6-foot-3 Kiki Iriafen, 6-foot-5 Shakira Austin and 6-foot-7 Lauren Betts — combined for 50 points and 19 rebounds, more than making up for the 38 and seven they conceded to Aces legend A’ja Wilson. Meantime, guard Sonia Citron poured in 20 points (along with eight assists), with 11 of them coming in the decisive fourth quarter, when Citron, who typically plays off the ball, shifted to point guard and the Mystics stormed back from nine points down in the final four minutes.

The victory over the Aces made the Mystics the only team this season with wins over all three of the league’s top teams: Minnesota, Golden State and Las Vegas. Regardless of where they finish in the standings, they have become that team no one would want to face in the playoffs.

Lauren Betts Mystics AP - 26169655043560 (3236x2157, AR: 1.50)
“We don’t make it a secret: We want to make the playoffs. We want to make a push,” said point guard Georgia Amoore, who scored 10 on Wednesday. “We’re not that team that other teams can relax against, or take a night off against. We’ve proven that.”

The next stop for Iriafen, Citron and Austin is Chicago, where Iriafen and Citron — the first WNBA teammates in 27 years to earn All-Star berths in each of their first two seasons — will be on opposite squads for the game itself, while Austin, a notable snub in All-Star selections, will participate in Friday night’s Shooting Stars competition.

The Mystics’ sooner-than-expected arrival as a playoff threat and their enviable collection of young talent — the 25-year-old Austin and 26-year-old forward Michaela Onyenwere are the only players on the roster with more than one and a half years of WNBA experience — has both given them the appearance of a nascent juggernaut and also made them an intriguing factor ahead of next month’s trade deadline.

Up to now, the Mystics have been pointed decidedly and aggressively in the direction of rebuilding, hoarding draft picks and emphasizing player development. A year ago at the trade deadline, sitting on a 13-15 record, they dealt away veteran guard and three-time All-Star Brittney Sykes, then finished the season on a 3-12 skid.

Might Washington take the opposite approach this summer, and perhaps spend some of its remaining draft capital and young talent on a veteran or two — in effect stopping the rebuild and turning this into a go-for-it year?

Among the team’s needs: a veteran point guard (the assortment of point guards on their roster have amassed -0.2 win shares this season) and/or a deadly three-point shooter (they rank next-to-last in the league in three-point attempts, makes and shooting percentage). Among the available targets: 35-year-old veteran and seven-time All-Star Skylar Diggins, whom the Chicago Sky may be shopping.

But the likelier play for the Mystics would be to stand pat at the deadline, let the season play out and make their next push this offseason via free agency and/or the draft. They already own Chicago’s first-round pick in 2027, which is likely to be high. That means the Mystics could have their choice of a game-changing talent like USC’s JuJu Watkins, Texas’ Madison Booker or Notre Dame’s Hannah Hidalgo.

The Mystics have been operating without a general manager since parting ways with Jamila Wideman in April, meaning Johnson and Michael Winger, president of basketball operations for Monumental Basketball, will be making the big calls on the Mystics’ direction and philosophy. On Wednesday, Johnson deflected a question about the team’s trade deadline strategy.

“Every player on our roster has gotten better. Every single one of them. And that has allowed us as a team to get better. And we’ll lift our heads up in August and just kind of see where we are,” Johnson said. “What we talked about at the start of the season, in terms of having a young group that was eager to get better, to grow individually and as a team — so far, so good. We’re on track in terms of taking a step forward. But the [2026] journey is only a little more than halfway through.”

Once they return from the All-Star break, the Mystics face a gauntlet of a schedule in the first half of August, including back-to-backs against both Dallas (currently fourth in the standings) and Las Vegas (currently third). There is also another stretch of six games in 11 days featuring another pair of cross-country flights.

Which means before Johnson and the Mystics can look too far down the road, he still has one Odyssey to face at the cinema and another on the basketball court.
entries.author: Dave Sheinin

entries.title: Mike Johnson is ‘Sick of This Shit’ (But Sorry He Said So)
entries.summary: Most House Republicans are frustrated that a small band of conservatives are upending the party’s agenda, yet they face few consequences.
entries.content:
Speaker Mike Johnson was at his wit’s end.

For months, he had been dealing with one rebellion after another, and now members were about to tank a bipartisan veterans bill. The House was scheduled to quickly approve the bill that Thursday morning and head out for the weekend.

Trying to salvage another priority for his party, Johnson brought a handful of members, including those threatening to block the bill, into his “ceremonial room” across from the House chamber. Reps. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Florida), who opposed the bill, and Zach Nunn (R-Iowa), who supported it, started yelling at each other.

Luna then pointed her anger toward Johnson. Fed up, the speaker snapped and replied, “I’m sick of this shit,” according to multiple sources in the room.

Witnesses were shocked that the typically even-keeled Johnson had lost his cool. Almost immediately, he apologized to Luna for his outburst. He then walked over to the elementary-school-aged son of Rep. Gabe Evans (R-Colorado), who had witnessed the interaction, and got down on one knee and apologized for cursing in front of him, the sources said.

Johnson left the room and did what he’s been forced to do repeatedly this Congress: pull the bill because a few Republicans wouldn't agree to vote for it.

NOTUS spoke with more than a dozen lawmakers and aides for a broader view of how the speaker’s daily crises — often brought about by his own members — continue to derail his party’s agenda.

Most rank-and-file Republican members are upset with the handful who regularly make the House look like a hot mess. Some lawmakers refuse to be team players, and the incentive structure that rewards them makes governing impossible, they say. (Proposals that would punish those who step out of line are even being considered, sources told NOTUS.)

“It creates anger and resentment,” retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Nebraska) said. “We want to get things done, and dysfunction’s not good.”

Republicans have shut down the House floor, tanked rules, cursed at one another on the floor and gotten in each other's faces — and those are just the fights that have happened in public.

In private, members have grown increasingly incensed at the state of the House of Representatives. And the episode between Luna and Johnson off of the House floor encapsulated that.

Johnson and House Republicans have managed, with a razor-thin majority, to pass significant legislation, but it hasn’t been easy or pretty. This week the conference passed three marquee bills — the annual defense authorization bill, a budget resolution for defense and farm aid and a bill curbing lawmakers from trading individual stocks.

But even these items came with significant hand-wringing and last-minute agita.

A handful of members — particularly those on the far right — have learned they can use their votes as leverage to get what they want. Johnson has frequently placated most of their demands, much to the dismay of the rest of the conference.

“The Republican conference is a diverse gathering of people, some of whom are really effective at getting things done and others who are more interested in knocking things down,” Rep. Dusty Johnson (R-South Dakota) told NOTUS.

As the House starts its annual August recess, members are fed up that the rebels are being rewarded for their bad behavior.
Mike Johnson (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)“The vast majority of members are team players who do not appreciate the minority, the small minority, that does that,” Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R-Florida) said of the members who block legislation. “I don’t appreciate it, but we live in that reality that they can leverage it. So there are the vast majority of us who don’t like that. We're team players.”

But the group that’s spent this year holding things up view themselves as fighting for conservative principles.

“It’s the hardcore conservatives against everybody else,” Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tennessee) said. “Matt Gaetz told me, I remember, he said that, ‘We'll have more power if we don't have a supermajority; it gives us more opportunity because if we did, we’d just get run over,’” referring to the former House Republican who regularly clashed with top leaders.

Rep. Andy Harris (R-Maryland), the chair of the House Freedom Caucus, said “the only measure is whether we are successful in delivering for the American people.”

Members across the Republican conference agree on one thing: Johnson has the hardest job in Washington. Gimenez described Johnson as being in a “very difficult situation” and said, "It's tough to herd cats.”

“So while some of us may be frustrated by some of the actions, it's not by his actions. It's merely by the actions of those few,” Gimenez added.

Bacon agreed, noting that with just a two-seat majority, “there's not a lot of leeway.”

“They should be adults and be responsible. So it's really the individuals versus Mike. I mean, Mike can only do so much,” he said.
Anna Paulina Luna (5125x3417, AR: 1.50)Earlier in the summer, Luna and a handful of other members shut down the House floor for more than two weeks over President Donald Trump’s priority voting bill that’s going nowhere in the Senate. Johnson eventually gave Luna a commitment the House would attach the bill to must-pass legislation in an attempt to force the Senate’s hand.

In the past, lawmakers who rebelled against the speaker were punished; they lost a plum committee assignment or leaders refused to advance their bills. Now, with such a narrow majority, members believe there’s not much leadership can really do.

“You have a chicken-and-egg situation,” one GOP member said. “There's really no ability to lay consequences on someone's feet when you need them again next week.”

This House Republican said the way it typically plays out is unfair to everyone else.

“You’ve seen the speaker and the leadership spend a wildly disproportionate amount of time with a narrow band of members. And, you know, that hasn't necessarily sat well with the couple that come here, work together, work hard and are trying to move their own objectives forward,” they said.

But some members told NOTUS that Johnson is being an enabler by agreeing to almost every demand.

“They get accommodated a lot, and we don't like it,” Bacon said.

The constant cycle of rebels getting away with stalling Republican bills is prompting some members to come up with ways to punish them, sources tell NOTUS.

When then-Speaker Paul Ryan faced challenges from those in the Freedom Caucus, Rep. Austin Scott (R-Georgia) proposed a rule that if any Republican voted procedurally with the Democrats and blocked legislation from coming to the floor, then the GOP-led steering committee — a panel that doles out committee assignments — could take action against the member by removing them from a committee or stripping them of a gavel.
Rep. Austin Scott (6038x4025, AR: 1.50)Ryan ultimately rebuffed the plan. But now, Scott has revived the idea as a measure of accountability and is pitching his colleagues on it, two members with knowledge of the discussions told NOTUS.

“It’s clear these guys are no longer representing their districts,” one of those Republican members told NOTUS. “So this would provide more to be put [on] the steering committee, not a speaker who effectively has a gun to his head every time he makes a decision.”

Without any real ability to penalize lawmakers, Johnson has had to find different ways to keep his members in line. One strategy has been to make promises he can’t always keep.

Back in June, Johnson promised hard-line conservatives a vote on a controversial immigration bill known as “HR 2” before the July 4 recess, but that upset more moderate members who didn’t want to vote on the bill in an election year.

In turn, Johnson ended up not putting the bill up for a vote, which caused a ripple effect of drama.

The speaker has also promised to include members’ wish lists in subsequent reconciliation packages as a way to punt fights to a later time.

In 2025, when members were upset that their priorities weren’t in the first reconciliation bill, Johnson assured them they would be included in the second party-line package the conference was planning to vote on in 2026. When that bill became narrowly focused on funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol, the speaker promised those same members that their issues would be addressed in a third reconciliation bill.
Mike Johnson (5555x3703, AR: 1.50)But the White House has instead commandeered that package to be for Iran war funding, aid for farmers and portions of the SAVE America Act.

“Unfortunately, the call has been made,” said Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas), who was the top Republican pushing for a larger reconciliation package that could have included policies tackling prescription-drug costs, energy affordability and fraud prevention.

Burchett said the promise of another party-line bill is “a moving target” and that “it’s frustrating” when the goal keeps moving.

One senior GOP member said Johsnon is acting as “a military tactician” when it comes to lining up legislation. “In order to hold the front line together, the speaker has been strategically retreating across the calendar,” the senior Republican said.

But at some point, the speaker will have to face the political realities of making members potentially vote for another sprawling reconciliation package, and that could impact his own future.

“Will the great political battle come in September or after the November general election? I cannot say,” the member said. “But it is coming.”
entries.author: Reese Gorman
